capture.final_message:
Use the standard characterization of \(\aleph_0\): a cardinal is below \(\aleph_0\) exactly when it is finite.

- Apply this directly to show every natural cardinal \(n\) is \(<\aleph_0\), proving the first conjunct.
- For the left side of the inner `Iff`, use the same characterization: `[Finite α]` implies `Cardinal.mk α < Cardinal.aleph0`.
- For the right side, pass from a set \(s\) to its subtype `Set.Elem α s`. Interpret `Set.Countable s` as countability of this subtype and `Set.Infinite s` as its infinitude. Then use the standard classification that a type is denumerable precisely when it is both countable and infinite.

Both sides of the inner `Iff` are thus established independently, so organize that `Iff` by proving each side outright rather than deriving either substantive statement from the other. The only technical bookkeeping is installing the countability and infinitude propositions as local typeclass instances when constructing `Nonempty (Denumerable (Set.Elem α s))`.
